subject: physics

items.q: Which statement gives the definition of power?
items.correct: The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done
items.misconception: The total amount of energy that a device transfers
items.why: In everyday speech 'powerful' means big or strong, and both energy and power are introduced with the word 'transfer'. The division by time is easy to drop. Read the definition as a rate: power = (energy transferred)/(time). Two values are always needed. 1000 J in 1 s is a power of 1000 W; the same 1000 J spread over 100 s is only 10 W.
items.random_wrong: The time that an energy transfer takes to finish

items.q: Which word equation for power is given in the specification?
items.why: Any pair of quantities in one equation is assumed to rise together, and the difference between a numerator and a denominator is not checked. Test with numbers: 600 J in 10 s is 60 W, but 600 J in 20 s is only 30 W.

items.q: In the equation P = E/t, which units should be used for E and for t?
items.correct: energy in joules and time in seconds
items.misconception: energy in newtons and time in seconds
items.why: Work is introduced through force multiplied by distance, so the newton stays attached to it, and the shared symbol W pulls students towards watts. The specification states work done, W, in joules, J. Newtons measure force; watts measure power.
items.random_wrong: energy in watts and time in seconds

items.q: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of:
items.why: Both units appear together in the same equation, and labels such as '2000 W kettle' and 'joules of energy' are met at different times, so the pairing is never fixed. Fix the pairing from the specification: power, P, in watts, W; energy transferred, E, in joules, J. The watt already contains 'per second'.

items.q: A kettle transfers 360 000 J of energy in 180 s. What is its power?
items.why: The student remembers that power involves an energy and a time but not their order, and 'it takes longer, so more power' matches the everyday idea that hard jobs need power. Think in joules per second: the energy goes on top. A device that takes longer to transfer the same energy is less powerful, not more.

items.q: A crane does 90 000 J of work in 30 s. What is the power of the crane?
items.why: In everyday speech 'powerful' means big or strong, and both energy and power are introduced with the word 'transfer'. The division by time is easy to drop. Read the definition as a rate: power = (energy transferred)/(time). Two values are always needed. 1000 J in 1 s is a power of 1000 W; the same 1000 J spread over 100 s is only 10 W.

items.q: Two electric motors lift identical loads through the same height. Motor A takes 4 s and motor B takes 10 s. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Motor A is more powerful, because it does the same work in a shorter time
items.misconception: Motor A is more powerful, because it must have done extra work on the load
items.why: Speed is read as effort, so a machine that finishes sooner is assumed to have put more in, and work done and power are not held apart. Separate the two quantities: the work done is fixed by the load and the height, while the power depends on how long that work takes.
items.random_wrong: Motor B is more powerful, because it keeps working for a longer time

items.q: A 1500 W heater is switched on for 300 s. How much energy does it transfer?
items.why: Students rearrange by pattern-matching rather than by operation, moving whichever symbol they want to the front while leaving the division sign where it was. Multiply both sides of P = E/t by t to get Pt = E. Check with units: watts multiplied by seconds gives joules, watts divided by seconds does not.

items.q: The specification gives the equation P = W/t. What does W stand for in this equation?
items.correct: the work done, measured in joules
items.misconception: the power in watts, as W is its unit
items.why: The symbol for the unit of power and the symbol for work done are the same letter, and students match letters to units before checking which quantity is meant. Read the specification pairing: work done, W, in joules, J. A unit never appears as a quantity on the right-hand side of an equation.
items.random_wrong: the work done, measured in newtons

items.q: A motor transfers 15 000 J of energy in 2 minutes. What is its power?
items.why: The equation is remembered as a rule for numbers rather than for quantities, and the unit line 'time, t, in seconds, s' is treated as background information. Convert first, then substitute: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600. A power that comes out 60 times too big is the signature of this slip.

items.q: A lamp transfers 500 J of energy while a pump does 500 J of work. Which statement about the units is correct?
items.correct: Both are in joules, because doing work is a way of transferring energy
items.misconception: Work done is in newtons, so the two quantities cannot be compared
items.why: Work is introduced through force multiplied by distance, so the newton stays attached to it, and the shared symbol W pulls students towards watts. The specification states work done, W, in joules, J. Newtons measure force; watts measure power.
items.random_wrong: Energy transferred is in watts, so only the work is in joules

items.q: Two cranes lift the same load to the same height. Crane X takes 20 s and crane Y takes 50 s. Which quantity is different for the two cranes?
items.correct: the power of the two cranes
items.misconception: the work done on the load
items.why: Speed is read as effort, so a machine that finishes sooner is assumed to have put more in, and work done and power are not held apart. Separate the two quantities: the work done is fixed by the load and the height, while the power depends on how long that work takes.
items.random_wrong: the energy passed to the load

items.q: Is 1 joule the same as 1 watt?
items.correct: An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt. A joule on its own is not a watt.
items.misconception: 1 J = 1 W, so the two units can be swapped freely, and larger multiples can be used just as loosely.
items.why: The words 'per second' are dropped when the relationship is memorised, leaving what looks like a plain equality between two units. Always say the full statement: one joule per second equals one watt. Writing 1 W = 1 J/s keeps the time in view, and keeps 1 W distinct from 1 kW.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In P = E/t, which quantity is measured in watts?
items.correct: Only P is in watts. E is in joules and t is in seconds.
items.misconception: The units can be attached to whichever symbol looks right, for example E in watts and P in joules.
items.why: The symbols P, E and W all begin unit names the student has met, and the labelling list is memorised as a block rather than symbol by symbol. Label the equation before substituting: P (W) = E (J) / t (s). Any answer for P must come out in watts.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does 'more powerful' just mean a motor can lift a heavier load?
items.correct: Power compares rates of energy transfer. Two motors lifting the same weight through the same height differ in power only because one takes less time.
items.misconception: Power is about how heavy a load a machine can move, or how big a force it exerts, not about how quickly it works.
items.why: Advertising uses 'powerful' for strength, and in most questions the loads differ, so weight rather than time is read as the deciding factor. Hold the load and the height fixed, as the specification example does, and the only difference left is the time taken.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.1.1.4 Power
